Hi Product Hunt! 👋 I’m Mateusz, the maker of Secret Key.

The problem: if something happens to you, your family is locked out of everything: email, photos, 2FA codes, crypto, bank. Most password managers offer no real way around that.

What Secret Key does: it protects your password database (e.g. KeePass) and splits the master password into pieces using Shamir’s Secret Sharing. You hand the pieces to people you trust, and you decide how many are needed to unlock it (for example, any 3 of 5). One piece alone reveals nothing.

How access works:

1.   A loved one signs in with their printed card.

2.   They confirm with an SMS code. [...] 2.   They confirm with an SMS code.

3.   The agreed number of people enter their pieces.

4.   A 48-hour timelock starts. You get an email with a one-click Panic Button to cut access off if it’s a false alarm.

5.   Only then can the vault be downloaded.

Details that matter:

   Self-hosted: it runs on your own server, so no vendor holds your vault.

   Pieces are generated offline, in your browser.

   Printable cards (PDF with QR code) for each person.

   Open source (MIT). [...] Open source (MIT).

🌐 Heads-up: the live demo (app.secretkey.website) and the app itself are currently in Polish only, since I built the system for my own family first. The video is narrated in Polish by default, but it comes with English narration, English subtitles and several other languages: just pick them on YouTube (⚙ → Audio track / Subtitles). The project site, documentation and the slides above are in English.

Shamir’s Secret Sharing is done with the open-source secrets.js library (MIT), the same one used by iancoleman.io/shamir, so you can verify the shares independently, outside Secret Key. Big thanks to its maintainers!

I’d love your feedback, especially on the recovery flow and what would make you trust a tool like this with your own vault. Thanks for checking it out! 🔑

results.title: The 2 Best Password Managers of 2026 | Reviews by Wirecutter
results.content:
It’s a good choice for families, too. When you set up a 1Password family plan, you put your passwords and other information in your shared vault instead of your personal vault to give access to everyone else on your plan. “Family organizers,” a group that includes the 1Password account that created your family’s account plus anyone they designate as a “family organizer,” can recover the accounts of other family members if they forget their master password or secret key, which is useful for helping kids or less technically inclined folks. 1Password recently added support for recovery codes, which can help ensure that you don’t get locked out of your account. If you want your account shared after death, storing the Emergency Kit printout in a shared safe or sharing the emergency backup [...] Tools to fix your security problems: Once your data is in your password manager, it should be able to identify weak, reused, and compromised passwords, and it should give you clear and easy-to-follow directions for changing them.
 Support for biometric logins: If your phone, tablet, or laptop has a fingerprint reader or face-scanning camera, you should be able to unlock your password manager with that, rather than a password or PIN, for convenience’s sake. [...] To protect your accounts, 1Password requires a “Secret Key” in addition to a password. It’s a bit confusing at first, but 1Password says it allows the company to better secure your data and ensure that attackers can’t steal the means to decrypt your vault from 1Password. (For details, you can read more about 1Password’s security model.) Previously, you had to enter the Secret Key each time you logged in on a new device, but 1Password now allows you to scan a QR code on a device where you’re already logged in; some of the 1Password apps can also import your Secret Key directly from your Emergency Kit PDF. Both new approaches are much easier, but you still might have to enter your password before you can enable biometric access, so keep that handy.
